children: By Lane Florsheim
WSJ. MAGAZINE
Bob Woodward has made a career of getting important, secretive people to reveal the hidden parts of their lives. He says that the best question is often a single syllable.
"A president will say, 'I did the following,' or, 'This is what took me to this point,'?" says the investigative journalist. "All you have to do is say, 'Why?'?"

The author of over 20 books, Woodward, 83, is coming out with his most personal project yet, a memoir called Secrets. In it, he reveals a number of his anonymous sources, including Hillary Clinton and several former Supreme Court justices. He shares documents from his files and details the experience of breaking the Watergate scandal in the 1970s and interviewing U.S. presidents including Gerald Ford, Barack Obama and Donald Trump. He also recounts painful memories from his childhood and happier ones from his marriage and fatherhood.

Woodward's assistant, Claire McMullen, helped him unpack these recollections during hours of interviews. "We recorded endless voice notes and she would say, 'What do you really feel? What's going through your head?' and push me in ways I unfortunately don't have the habit of pushing myself," he says.
Woodward lives in Washington, D.C., with his wife, the writer Elsa Walsh. Here, he discusses his caffeine routine and foolproof work philosophy.
What time do you get up on Mondays, and what's the first thing you do after waking up?

I try to wake up at 6 or 7 a.m. I'm embarrassed to say sometimes 8. At age 83, I think that's a luxury I still don't deserve. I look in the mirror while I'm brushing my teeth, and [on it] I have this love note from our younger daughter, Diana, and it's the first thing I see. "I love you both so much," smiley face, and then, "SHS and MABL." Now, SHS is a code that I have with our younger daughter: secret handshake, and "moon-and-back love," in other words, love you to the moon and back.
What do you do for coffee?
Coffee is very important. I make it strong, too strong according to my wife, Elsa, and anybody who drinks morning coffee with me, but it's the way I like it.
Do you eat breakfast?
Elsa calls me a labrador. I'll eat anything and too much of it.
What do you do for exercise?

I do a lot of exercise at this age. I do Pilates. I do physical therapy each day. I try to go out walking. I have had a couple of falls and broken some bones but I can now walk with a cane easily and sometimes dispose of the cane. I'd like to just break it.
What are your writing routines when you're working on a book?
Sometimes I'll work seven or eight hours. I think of it as, "Keep your a —  in the chair." Don't get up and wander around the house and do things. Much is accomplished when your a —  is in the chair.
Did going through that interview process with Claire change how you view writing about other subjects at all?

Yes, inevitably. People have a wall of resistance, and you have to get through it, and the key is time and patience and just not ever going for the throat or for a difficult context first, but actually going for: Who are you?
One of the things you're known for is your use of deep background sources. In Secrets, you reveal many of them for the first time. Why was this important to you?

The whole idea was to take readers as close as possible to the reporting process, and the reporting process has got to be slow and patient. With sources I had for decades, I was able to hold onto the relationship and never stop the flow of questions. People tolerate that. I'm not sure I would tolerate it.
You write about how Robert Redford spent weeks tailing you for All the President's Men. What was that like?

It was a little unnerving, quite frankly, but he was determined. He actually moved into the Madison Hotel across from the Washington Post, and when Redford and Alan Pakula, the director, were working on the script, they kept coming with questions. "What are you doing? Why are you doing that? Who are you?"
Do you feel like he captured it and you?
Never enough, never.
You write that the secret to impactful reporting throughout your life has been through collaborations.

Oh, first Carl Bernstein. Bob Costa. Claire, who has a law degree. Bless her, she went through my files; I had 500 boxes. We couldn't look at them all, but we looked at hundreds, and she would find my memos that I wrote, handwritten notes, the ingredients of the stories.
One of your reporting principles is to treat your subjects as seriously as they take themselves. Is that ever hard to do?

No, no, no, no, because I'm fascinated with the business of reporting. Even as early as age 8, I was suspicious of things. I became a snoop. I found all kinds of family secrets in my father's sock drawer.
What's your relationship with your phone like?
Too much. Like everyone, you have idle time and you look at it, but at home I have a landline. I ask people to call me on my landline because I can put it on speaker.
You write touchingly about Elsa throughout the book. Do you have something you consider the secret to a happy marriage?

We've been married for decades and have a daughter together. Elsa was a reporter at the Washington Post and a staff writer at the New Yorker, and she always has questions. I realized I'm positioned better in our relationship if I anticipate the questions and give her the answers. Probably the best relationship is when you share everything.
Do you have something you consider your most prized possession?

In a way, my office here, because it's books going way back, new books, pictures. I have a picture over here of my oldest daughter, Tali, who's 50, and the picture is of her saluting, and she's 5 or 6. I don't think it's a salute of obedience. There's an element made of mockery, that sort of relationship.
What's a piece of advice you've gotten that's guided or been important to you in life?

One of the solid pieces of advice I got with Carl Bernstein was from Katharine Graham, owner and publisher of the Post. She wrote to us at one point: "Well, Nixon's gone. You did some of the stories. Now don't start thinking too highly of yourselves, and let me give you a piece of advice: Beware of the demon pomposity."
Morning Must-Haves
Toothbrush "I have to brush my teeth."
Coffee "I can only drink about two cups in the morning and then I really should go cold turkey."
Kiss "A real sincere deep kiss from my wife."
Newspaper "I obviously use the internet, but there's something about the hard copy of the paper."
